warmup.q: A dump shows a thread in state RUNNABLE, with sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0 at the top of its stack. A second dump, 5 seconds later, shows the same stack and the same cpu=25.09ms. What is the thread doing?
options: Burning a CPU core in a tight loop
Waiting for bytes from the network: the JVM reports a thread in native code as RUNNABLE even while the operating system has it asleep
Nothing: the dump is wrong, because a RUNNABLE thread always uses CPU
warmup.why: The JVM can't see inside native code, so a thread in a native socket read counts as RUNNABLE. Its CPU time didn't move in 5 seconds, so it isn't computing: the kernel has it asleep until data arrives. A busy loop would add thousands of milliseconds of CPU, and a deadlock shows BLOCKED or parked threads with lock lines.

opening:
Picture the restaurant at the worst moment of a night: nothing is leaving the kitchen. You can't stop the evening to question every cook, but you can take a photo through the door. In it, four waiters queue at the counter for the one order book. A cook stands at the back door with that book under his arm, waiting for a delivery. Another cook stirs a pot so hard it splashes. One photo can't say who is stuck and who is busy. Three photos, ten seconds apart, can.

A thread dump is that photo of a JVM: every thread, what it's doing, and which lock it holds or wants. The trap is to read one dump and trust the word RUNNABLE. In this lesson's demo, the thread holding everyone up is RUNNABLE and uses no CPU at all.

Lesson 7's loop barely sees threads that wait. In this lesson, we'll take dumps of a frozen report service, read one thread line by line, tell a waiting thread from a busy one, follow a lock to its owner and compare dumps over time. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with three photos of a kitchen where nothing moved: waiters queued for the order book, a cook at the back door holding it, another stirring without end. The service's dumps said the same: four BLOCKED workers, a RUNNABLE owner with flat CPU, one hot loop.

That closes the track, which began with a new cook reading every recipe card line by line. We watched the JIT learn, measured it fairly, and found where a running program spends its time and where it waits.

Now search your code for a synchronized block or lock() that calls the network before letting go.

Next, we'll look at a program's first seconds: why does a JVM start slowly, and how do you measure it?

sections.h: A thread dump is every stack, printed at one safepoint
sections.html:
Meet the patient. FrozenService is the report service on a bad day, stuck in five ways at once. A thread refreshes the catalog, the service's list of every document and the shelf it's on, while holding the catalog's lock. It asks the document store for the new list, and the store never answers. Four report workers need the same lock. There's also an idle pool, a busy loop, a second kind of lock, and 10,200 virtual threads. Run it, and it waits for you to look.

A thread dump is a printout of every thread in the JVM at one moment. (A thread is one line of work inside a program.) For each one it shows the name, the state, the stack of method calls it's in, and the locks it holds or wants. jcmd <pid> Thread.print asks the JVM for one. jcmd is the JDK tool that sends commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is the process id the operating system gave it. The JVM stops every Java thread at a safepoint, a point where it knows the full state of each frame (lesson 6 showed why profilers need one). While the threads stand still, it walks each stack and prints it, and then they all run on.

That pause is the photo's flash. With -Xlog:safepoint on JDK 25, the safepoint called PrintThreads took 36 to 74 ms for 28 threads on this busy 4-core machine. That's fine a few times on a live service. jstack <pid> prints the same dump.

jcmd                                    # lists Java processes and their PIDs
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-1.txt # every platform thread, plus the java.util.concurrent locks each one owns

Take the dump before anyone restarts a frozen service, because a restart throws the evidence away. If jcmd can't attach (it must run as the same operating-system user as the JVM), kill -3 <pid> sends the signal SIGQUIT, and the JVM prints the same dump to its own standard output.

Here's one thread from a real dump of the demo on JDK 25:

"report-worker-3" #24 [25043] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.36ms elapsed=11.19s tid=0x00007ff4242e2bc0 nid=25043 waiting for monitor entry  [0x00007ff40888d000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
	at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.writeReport(FrozenService.kt:54)
	- waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object)
	at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$1$0(FrozenService.kt:32)
	at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt$$Lambda/0x000000001e083000.run(Unknown Source)
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1090)
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:614)
	at java.lang.Thread.runWith(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:1487)
	at java.lang.Thread.run(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:1474)

Read each thread in this order.

  1. The name. report-worker-3 says which pool and which job, which is why the executors track had you name your threads. Unnamed threads all look like pool-3-thread-7.
  2. The state line. BLOCKED (on object monitor) means it wants to enter a synchronized block that another thread is inside. A monitor is the lock behind synchronized.
  3. The frames, top first, down to the first line of your own code: FrozenService.kt:54. That's where it is now. The frames below say how it got there.
  4. The lock lines, which start with -. - locked <a> means it holds the monitor of object a. - waiting to lock <a> means it wants it. - parking to wait for <a> means a java.util.concurrent lock, condition or queue has parked it, put it to sleep until someone wakes it. - waiting on <a> means it's inside Object.wait() and has given a back.

The number in <0x0000000735c08070> is the object's address in the heap at that moment. Inside one dump, the same address means the same object. Between dumps, a garbage collection, the JVM's clean-up of unused memory, may have moved the object. So don't match addresses across dumps.

Take the dump before you restart. Read each thread by name, state, first frame of your code, then its lock lines.

Check yourself: in one dump, four threads show - waiting to lock with the same address, and no thread shows - locked with it. What does that mean? (A thread holding it would show - locked. If none does, the lock was released a moment ago, and the next dump will tell.)

The demo's busiest-looking threads say RUNNABLE. That word deserves a closer look.

try.title: Take your first dump
steps: Run the demo. It prints its PID and stays frozen for 120 seconds (pass -Pargs=300 for longer).
In a second terminal, run jcmd to confirm the PID, then jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-1.txt.
Predict before you look: which state will the four report-worker threads be in, and at which line of FrozenService.kt?
Open dump-1.txt. Find the four report-worker threads, their state line, their first frame in workbench.performance.l08 and the address they wait for. Then search for vt-report.

code.title: FrozenService.kt
code.html: package workbench.performance.l08 import java.net.ServerSocket import java.net.Socket import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.withLock import kotlin.system.exitProcess // A report service that is stuck in five different ways at once, so a thread dump has something to show. // Run it, then take dumps from a second terminal while it waits. private val catalog = Any() private val archiveLock = ReentrantLock() @Volatile private var sink = 0L fun main(args: Array<String>) { val seconds = args.firstOrNull()?.toLong() ?: 120 // the "document store": the kernel accepts connections into the backlog, but nobody ever answers val store = ServerSocket(0) // 1. refreshes the catalog while holding its lock, and waits for an answer that never comes Thread.ofPlatform().name("catalog-refresh").start { synchronized(catalog) { Socket("localhost", store.localPort).use { it.getInputStream().read() } } } Thread.sleep(200) // 2. four report workers that need the same lock val reports = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("report-worker-", 1).factory()) repeat(4) { reports.execute { writeReport() } } // 3. an idle pool with nothing to do val exports = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("export-worker-", 1).factory()) repeat(2) { exports.execute { } } // 4. a hot loop Thread.ofPlatform().name("index-rebuild").start { rebuildIndex() } // 5. a ReentrantLock held by a thread that sleeps, and a thread that waits for it Thread.ofPlatform().name("archive-writer").start { archiveLock.withLock { Thread.sleep(600_000) } } Thread.sleep(100) Thread.ofPlatform().name("archive-reader").start { archiveLock.withLock { } } // 6. virtual threads: 10,000 waiting for a permit that never comes, 200 asleep val permits = Semaphore(0) repeat(10_000) { Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-report").start { permits.acquire() } } repeat(200) { Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-poll").start { Thread.sleep(600_000) } } println("PID ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()}: frozen for $seconds s. Take your dumps now.") // a daemon timer ends the demo; main returns, so it doesn't show up in the dumps Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("demo-timer").factory()) .schedule({ exitProcess(0) }, seconds, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } private fun writeReport() { synchronized(catalog) { sink++ } } private fun rebuildIndex() { var x = 1L while (true) { x = x * 6364136223846793005L + 1442695040888963407L if (x == 42L) sink = x } }

Take your dumps now."); // a daemon timer ends the demo; main returns, so it doesn't show up in the dumps Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("demo-timer").factory()) .schedule(() -> System.exit(0), seconds, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } private static void writeReport() { synchronized (catalog) { sink++; } } private static void rebuildIndex() { long x = 1; while (true) { x = x * 6364136223846793005L + 1442695040888963407L; if (x == 42L) sink = x; } } }

try.expect: The four report-worker threads are BLOCKED (on object monitor) in writeReport at FrozenService.kt:54, and all of them wait to lock the same address. There's no main thread (it returned) and no vt-report at all: Thread.print lists only platform threads. Section 4 deals with the virtual ones. In the Java version the line numbers differ, and the frames say FrozenServiceJava.

sections.h: RUNNABLE doesn't mean busy: compare cpu= between dumps
sections.html:
Both of these threads are RUNNABLE. One is burning a CPU core, and the other is asleep:

"catalog-refresh" #21 [25040] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=25.09ms elapsed=11.41s tid=0x00007ff4242d8600 nid=25040 runnable  [0x00007ff408b8d000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method)

"index-rebuild" #28 [25047] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=4089.43ms elapsed=11.18s tid=0x00007ff4242e7ac0 nid=25047 runnable  [0x00007ff40848c000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.rebuildIndex(FrozenService.kt:61)

The state is what the JVM knows, and the JVM can't see inside native code, code that runs outside Java in the operating system. When a thread calls a native method like read0, the JVM marks it "in native" and reports RUNNABLE, because that native code could be computing. Here the kernel, the core of the operating system, has the thread asleep until bytes arrive from the network. That's the cook at the back door: standing at his post, doing nothing. RUNNABLE means "not waiting for a Java lock", not "using the CPU".

The cpu= field tells them apart. It's the CPU time the operating system has charged to that thread since it started, the cook's step counter. One value means little. The change between two dumps says what the thread did in between. In the second dump, 5.6 seconds later, catalog-refresh still shows cpu=25.09ms: it used nothing. index-rebuild went from 4,089.43 ms to 6,288.02 ms while elapsed went from 11.18 s to 16.82 s. That's 2.2 seconds of CPU in 5.6 seconds, about 39% of one core. On a quiet machine it would be close to 100%. This one was shared with more than 30 busy programs.

On Linux, top -H -p <pid> shows the same thing per thread, live:

  PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
25047 root      20   0 7219012 186784  23404 R  80.0   1.1   0:12.57 index-rebuild
25014 root      20   0 7219012 186784  23404 S   0.0   1.1   0:00.00 java

The PID column of top -H is the Linux thread id. It's the same number as nid= and the number in brackets in the dump, so you can search the dump for nid=25047. Since JDK 18 the dump prints nid in decimal (change JDK-8268425). JDK 17 and older print it in hex, nid=0x61d7, so convert first with printf '%x\n' 25047. The JVM also gives each operating-system thread its Java name, cut to 15 characters, so top often shows the name straight away.

Inside a container you may not have top. Two dumps and cpu= work everywhere.

Check yourself: a thread shows the same stack in two dumps 5 seconds apart, and its cpu= grew by 4,900 ms. Is it stuck? (No. It's hot: a loop that never leaves that frame.)

catalog-refresh isn't stuck in the usual sense, then. It's waiting, and it's holding something while it waits.

steps: With the demo still running, take a second dump about 5 seconds after the first: jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-2.txt.
Predict: which of catalog-refresh and index-rebuild will show more CPU in the second dump?

sections.h: Follow the lock to the thread that holds everyone up
sections.html:
Four report-worker threads waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> are a queue at one door. The question is who's inside. Search the same dump for that address with - locked:

"catalog-refresh" #21 [25040] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=25.09ms elapsed=11.41s tid=0x00007ff4242d8600 nid=25040 runnable  [0x00007ff408b8d000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method)
	...
	at java.net.Socket$SocketInputStream.read(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Socket.java:958)
	at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$0(FrozenService.kt:26)
	- locked <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object)

The - locked line sits under the frame that entered synchronized. So catalog-refresh took the catalog lock in its own code, then called the document store, and is waiting for an answer with the lock still held. Every report that needs the catalog now waits for the store. That's the cook at the back door with the order book under his arm. The fix isn't in the four blocked threads. Make the slow call outside the lock, give the socket a read timeout, and take the lock only to swap in the result.

A ReentrantLock, the JDK's other kind of lock, shows up differently. The waiter says - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync), but its owner prints no - locked line, because a ReentrantLock isn't tied to a stack frame. That's what -l is for: it ends each thread with the java.util.concurrent locks it owns.

"archive-writer" #29 [25048] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.19ms elapsed=11.18s ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x0000000735c10a88> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)

Without -l, you can see that archive-reader waits, but not for whom. catalog-refresh lists one too: the socket's own read lock inside NioSocketImpl. A thread can hold several locks.

Keep following. The owner may itself wait for another lock, and so on. If the chain comes back to a thread you already passed, it's a deadlock, two cooks each holding the pan the other needs. The JVM checks for that while it prints, and adds Found one Java-level deadlock at the end of the dump, with both threads.

Not every parked thread is stuck. An idle pool thread, such as export-worker-1, shows - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.AbstractQueuedSynchronizer$ConditionObject) under LinkedBlockingQueue.take and ThreadPoolExecutor.getTask. A condition has no owner, so the chain ends there. It's a worker waiting for a task, leaning on the wall, and none of your code is in its stack.

Follow every wait to its owner, and fix the owner. The queue is only the symptom.

Check yourself: 30 threads are parked inside your connection pool's getConnection, and no thread holds a lock they want. What doesn't the dump show you? (Who holds the 20 connections. Look for the threads whose stacks show they're using one, for example inside a database call.)

A photo shows where everyone stands. It can't show who's moving.

refs.title: JEP 444: Virtual Threads (the new thread dump format)

sections.h: One dump is a photo: take three, and group thousands
sections.html:
One dump is a photo. A thread caught in a database call might finish 2 ms later. Take three, a few seconds apart, and compare each thread across them:

for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > dump-$i.txt; sleep 5; done
Same frames in every dump? CPU grew? Your code in the stack? What it is
yes no yes Stuck: waiting for a lock, a socket or a queue. Follow its lock line.
yes yes yes Hot: a loop that never leaves that frame
no either yes Working: it moves through the code
yes no no Idle: a pool or JVM thread waiting for work

This lesson's lab turns that table into code.

One caution about hot threads. The dump stops threads at safepoints, so a hot thread's top frame is where it reached the next safepoint poll, not always the line that costs the most. That's the safepoint bias from lesson 6. In index-rebuild the whole loop is one line, so the dump is right. In a big method, confirm with async-profiler.

Now the virtual threads, the JDK's lightweight threads that run on a few ordinary ones. The demo started 10,000 virtual threads that wait for a permit and 200 that sleep. Thread.print shows none of them, only the four idle carrier threads, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 to -4, that would run them. In the kitchen, the photo shows the cooks and not the order tickets pinned on the rail. Virtual threads need the newer dump format that came with them (JEP 444):

jcmd $PID Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/threads.txt                 # plain text, includes virtual threads
jcmd $PID Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json   # the same, for tools

On JDK 25 each virtual thread looks like this. On JDK 21 the first line has no state, and there are no lock lines:

#32 "vt-report" virtual WAITING 2026-11-17T08:09:26.520624548Z
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:745)
    - parking to wait for <java.util.concurrent.Semaphore$NonfairSync@4deadc8d>
    at java.base/java.lang.System$1.parkVirtualThread(System.java:2285)

Nobody reads 10,200 stacks. Group them by the first frame of your own code, and read the biggest group:

awk 'BEGIN { RS = ""; FS = "\n" } / virtual / { for (i = 2; i <= NF; i++) if ($i ~ /workbench\./) { n[$i]++; break } } END { for (k in n) print n[k], k }' /tmp/threads.txt | sort -rn

10000     at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$6$0(FrozenService.kt:44)
200     at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$7$0(FrozenService.kt:45)

Ten thousand reports wait at line 44, for a permit. That's your incident. The Javadoc of HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpThreads, which this command uses, says the dump includes every platform thread and "may include some or all virtual threads", so read the counts as close, not exact.

Check yourself: you take three dumps of a service on virtual threads, and the biggest group grows from 2,000 to 6,000 to 9,000 threads at the same frame. What do you know? (Requests arrive faster than that frame lets them through. Something downstream of it is slow or stuck.)

Here's the limit of a dump. It shows who waits, and for whom. It can't say why the document store doesn't answer, how long each call took, or what happened a minute ago. For that, go back to the recordings of lesson 5, and to the store's own evidence.

try.title: Group the virtual threads
steps: With the demo running, write the new dump format: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/threads.txt (add -overwrite if the file exists).
Predict: how many groups will the awk line print, and which is biggest?
Run the awk line from this section. Then count the virtual threads by state.

code.title: terminal 2
code.html: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -overwrite /tmp/threads.txt awk 'BEGIN { RS = ""; FS = "\n" } / virtual / { for (i = 2; i <= NF; i++) if ($i ~ /workbench\./) { n[$i]++; break } } END { for (k in n) print n[k], k }' /tmp/threads.txt | sort -rn # JDK 25: count virtual threads by state grep ' virtual ' /tmp/threads.txt | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c

try.expect: Two groups: 10,000 threads at FrozenService.kt:44 (waiting for a permit) and 200 at line 45 (asleep). On JDK 25 the state count says 10000 WAITING and 200 TIMED_WAITING. On JDK 21 the plain format has no state field, so the second count doesn't work.

compare.title: The cpu= column from inside the process, with ThreadMXBean

java.title: HotThreadsJava.java
java.html: package workbench.performance.l08; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadInfo; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; // The "cpu=" column of a thread dump, read from inside the process: which platform threads used CPU in the last interval? public class HotThreadsJava { record Hot(String name, long cpuNanos) { } static List<Hot> hottest(long millis, int n) throws InterruptedException { ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); Map<Long, Long> before = new HashMap<>(); for (long id : mx.getAllThreadIds()) before.put(id, mx.getThreadCpuTime(id)); // platform threads only Thread.sleep(millis); List<Hot> hot = new ArrayList<>(); for (long id : mx.getAllThreadIds()) { Long then = before.get(id); long now = mx.getThreadCpuTime(id); // -1 once a thread has died ThreadInfo info = mx.getThreadInfo(id); if (then != null && info != null && now > then) hot.add(new Hot(info.getThreadName(), now - then)); } hot.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Hot::cpuNanos).reversed()); return hot.subList(0, Math.min(n, hot.size())); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinner = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("index-rebuild").start(() -> { long x = 1; while (true) x = x * 31 + 7; }); for (Hot h : hottest(500, 3)) System.out.printf("%-20s %6.1f ms%n", h.name(), h.cpuNanos() / 1e6); } }

kotlin.title: HotThreads.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.performance.l08 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // The "cpu=" column of a thread dump, read from inside the process: which platform threads used CPU in the last interval? data class Hot(val name: String, val cpuNanos: Long) fun hottest(millis: Long, n: Int): List<Hot> { val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val before = mx.allThreadIds.associateWith { mx.getThreadCpuTime(it) } // platform threads only Thread.sleep(millis) return mx.allThreadIds.toList().mapNotNull { id -> val then = before[id] ?: return@mapNotNull null val now = mx.getThreadCpuTime(id) // -1 once a thread has died val name = mx.getThreadInfo(id)?.threadName ?: return@mapNotNull null if (now > then) Hot(name, now - then) else null }.sortedByDescending { it.cpuNanos }.take(n) } fun main() { Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("index-rebuild").start { var x = 1L while (true) x = x * 31 + 7 } for (h in hottest(500, 3)) println("%-20s %6.1f ms".format(h.name, h.cpuNanos / 1e6)) }

compare.note: Both read the same JVM counters that a dump prints as cpu=: sample every thread's CPU time, wait, sample again, and sort by the difference. That's a cheap health check that answers "which thread is hot" without top. The behavior is the same. Kotlin's associateWith and mapNotNull replace the two loops, and since LongArray has no mapNotNull, the Kotlin version calls toList() first. One limit applies to both, checked on JDK 21 and 25: getAllThreadIds() lists only platform threads, and getThreadCpuTime returns -1 for a virtual thread. For virtual threads, look at the carrier threads' CPU, or use a profiler.

worked.title: Three dumps of a frozen service, read in five minutes

steps.say: 1. Capture the evidence before anyone restarts anything: three dumps, 5 seconds apart, each in its own file.
steps.code: PID=$(pgrep -f FrozenService | head -1) for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > dump-$i.txt; sleep 5; done

steps.say: 1. Count the states to see the shape. Four BLOCKED threads in a service that should never wait long for a monitor is the first lead. The 12 RUNNABLE ones include JVM threads and threads in native calls, so they prove nothing yet.
steps.code: grep -h 'java.lang.Thread.State' dump-1.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # 12 java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE # 6 java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) # 4 java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) # 3 java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking) # ...

steps.say: 1. Ask what the BLOCKED threads want. One address four times means one door and one queue.
steps.code: grep -h 'waiting to lock' dump-1.txt | sort | uniq -c # 4 - waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object)

steps.say: 1. Find who holds it, then check whether the owner is working or waiting. Its stack ends in a socket read, and its CPU time is the same in all three dumps: it's waiting for the network with the lock held.
steps.code: awk '/^"/ { name = $1 } /- locked <0x0000000735c08070>/ { print name }' dump-1.txt # "catalog-refresh" grep -h '^"catalog-refresh"' dump-*.txt | grep -o 'cpu=[0-9.]*ms' # cpu=25.09ms # cpu=25.09ms # cpu=25.09ms

steps.say: 1. Fix the owner, not the queue. Make the slow call with a deadline and no lock held, then take the lock only to swap in the result. Now a slow store delays one refresh, not every report.
steps.code: CatalogData fresh = store.fetchCatalog(Duration.ofSeconds(2)); // 1. slow call: no lock held, with a deadline synchronized (catalog) { // 2. lock only to swap the data catalog.replace(fresh); }

alt.html: val fresh = store.fetchCatalog(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // 1. slow call: no lock held, with a deadline synchronized(catalog) { // 2. lock only to swap the data catalog.replace(fresh) }

lab.title: Read dumps in code: hot, blocked and stuck threads
steps: Read ThreadDump.kt. The parser is done: it turns each thread of a real Thread.print -l dump into a DumpedThread with its name, nid, state, cpuMs, frames, the locks it holds and the lock it waits for.

Open src/test/resources/workbench/performance/l08/dump-1.txt. It's a real dump of FrozenService on JDK 25, and dump-2.txt and dump-3.txt were taken about 5 and 11 seconds later. The two deadlock files come from a small program with two threads, merge-A and merge-B, that each lock one chapter and wait for the other's, plus two threads that are both called worker.

Run the tests: ten of the eleven fail (the one that checks the given parser passes). Write hottest: pair each thread in after with the same thread in before by nid, keep the ones whose CPU grew, biggest first, at most n. Run the tests: the three hottest tests should pass.
Write blockedChain: from the named thread, follow waitsFor to ownerOf, again and again, until a thread waits for nothing or a name comes back.
Write stuck: the threads that have the same frames in every dump, your code in the stack, and CPU growth under the budget. Run all the tests.
hints: before.byNid(now.nid) finds a thread's earlier self. A thread that started between the two dumps has none: skip it.
In blockedChain, thread.waitsFor?.let(dump::ownerOf) is the next thread in the chain, or null when the chain ends. An idle pool thread waits for a condition object, and nobody owns a condition.
For the cycle, check whether the owner's name is already in your list before you add it. Add it either way, then stop if it was there.
For stuck, start from the first dump's threads and look each one up in the others with byNid. == on two List<String> compares every frame. The CPU check needs only the first and the last dump.

drill.title: Group a virtual-thread dump from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write groupByFirstAppFrame(dump: String, appPrefix: String). It takes the text written by jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file and returns, biggest first, how many virtual threads have each first frame of your code. A blank line separates threads, and a virtual thread's first line contains virtual. Each frame line starts with at after its indentation.

answer.html: fun groupByFirstAppFrame(dump: String, appPrefix: String): List<Pair<String, Int>> = dump.split(Regex("\\n\\s*\\n")) // 1. one record per thread .map { it.trim() } .filter { record -> " virtual" in record.lineSequence().first() } // 2. only virtual threads .mapNotNull { record -> // 3. its first frame of your code record.lines().map { it.trim() }.firstOrNull { it.startsWith("at $appPrefix") } } .groupingBy { it }.eachCount() // 4. count per frame .toList() .sortedByDescending { it.second }

alt.html: static List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> groupByFirstAppFrame(String dump, String appPrefix) { return Arrays.stream(dump.split("\\n\\s*\\n")) // 1. one record per thread .map(String::trim) .filter(r -> r.lines().findFirst().orElse("").contains(" virtual")) // 2. only virtual threads .flatMap(r -> r.lines().map(String::trim) // 3. its first frame of your code .filter(l -> l.startsWith("at " + appPrefix)).limit(1)) .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(f -> f, Collectors.counting())) // 4. count per frame .entrySet().stream() .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()) .toList(); }

recap: jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l prints every platform thread's state, stack and locks at one safepoint. Take it before you restart, and use kill -3 if jcmd can't attach.
Read each thread by name, state, the first frame of your code, then the lock lines: locked, waiting to lock, parking to wait for, waiting on.
RUNNABLE only means "not waiting for a Java lock". Compare cpu= between two dumps, or use top -H, whose PID is the dump's nid (decimal since JDK 18).
For a blocked thread, follow the lock to its owner and fix the owner. For java.util.concurrent locks you need -l to see who owns them.

Take three dumps a few seconds apart: same frames and flat CPU means stuck, same frames and rising CPU means hot, and no frames of yours means idle. Virtual threads only appear in Thread.dump_to_file; group them by your first frame.
The limit: a dump shows who waits and for whom, at one moment. It can't say why the other side doesn't answer or how long calls took; that's what recordings (lesson 5) are for.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how you'd find out why a service has stopped answering, using only thread dumps. Say what you'd capture, what you'd compare, and how you'd decide which thread to fix.
explain.answer: Before anyone restarts it, I'd take three dumps with jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l, 5 seconds apart. In each thread I read the name, the state, the first frame of our code and the lock lines. I don't trust RUNNABLE, because threads in native socket reads are RUNNABLE too, so I compare cpu= between dumps. A thread whose CPU rises in the same frame is hot. For blocked or parked threads I follow the lock: the address on waiting to lock or parking to wait for leads to the thread that holds it, under - locked or, for a ReentrantLock, under Locked ownable synchronizers. I keep following until I reach a thread that waits for something outside the JVM, like a socket, or until the chain loops, which is a deadlock. That owner is what I fix. Threads with the same frames, flat CPU and none of our code are just idle pool threads. On virtual threads I'd use Thread.dump_to_file, group the threads by their first frame, and read the biggest group.

deeper.html:
The JSON format is what you'd feed a tool. On JDK 25 each thread has tid, name, state, stack, and lock fields: parkBlocker with the parked-on object and its owner thread id, blockedOn for a monitor a thread wants, waitingOn, and monitorsOwned. On JDK 21 a thread has only tid, name and stack. The JSON also groups threads by thread container: <root>, each thread pool, and each executor made by Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). In this lesson's demo, <root> holds 10,212 threads, because the demo starts its virtual threads with Thread.ofVirtual() directly, and each ThreadPoolExecutor holds its own workers. With virtual threads, that grouping often says more than the stacks do. The JSON also names owners: in the demo's file, archive-reader's parkBlocker gives its owner as thread 29, archive-writer, with no -l needed.

jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
jq '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | {container, threadCount}' /tmp/threads.json

Thread.print -e adds allocated= and defined_classes= to each header. That's another cheap way, besides JFR, to find the thread that allocates the most.

If the JVM is so stuck that it can't reach a safepoint, jcmd and kill -3 both hang, because both need one. The last resort is jhsdb jstack --pid <pid>. It reads the process from outside, like a debugger, so it needs permission to attach to the process (ptrace on Linux) and pauses the whole JVM while it reads. Use it only when the normal dump won't come.

In code, ThreadMXBean.dumpAllThreads(true, true) returns the same information as Thread.print -l as ThreadInfo objects, and findDeadlockedThreads() runs the deadlock check. Both cover platform threads only. A health check that runs findDeadlockedThreads() every minute costs a safepoint each time. On this busy machine one Thread.print safepoint took 36 to 74 ms, so measure before you add one to a service where every millisecond counts.
